analysis.one_liner: Cuts the federal tax on U.S. corporations' foreign profits to a flat 5%.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Steve Stockman in December 2014 with no cosponsors, died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently set the federal tax rate on profits that U.S. companies earn abroad at a flat 5%, down from the then-standard corporate rate of up to 35%. Its sponsor argued that companies were holding roughly a trillion dollars in profits overseas to avoid the higher rate, and that cutting the tax would bring that money home to create jobs. The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or another cosponsor before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: Multinational U.S. corporations with large foreign profits would gain the most: their tax on overseas earnings would drop from as high as 35% to a flat 5%, permanently. The bill's sponsor claimed the change would bring an estimated one trillion dollars of overseas profits back to the U.S. and could raise federal revenue by $50 billion, though this claim was not independently verified in the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a permanent flat 5% federal tax on earnings of U.S. companies with foreign operations, down from rates as high as 35% under then-current law.
Repeals the one-time framework of the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004, which had allowed a temporary 5.25% rate on repatriated earnings, and replaces it with a permanent 5% rate.
The bill states its goal is to bring roughly one trillion dollars of offshore corporate profits back to the United States, which its sponsor argued would spur jobs, capital investment, and research.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect far less tax on corporations' foreign profits, meaning the lost revenue would either reduce funding for public programs or shift the tax burden to other taxpayers. Companies that already paid the full rate on foreign earnings would also have gained an advantage over domestic-focused businesses.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the tax on foreign earnings from up to 35% to a permanent 5% would sharply reduce federal revenue from multinational corporations, with the lost amount made up by other taxpayers or by less government spending.

The bill's claim that a lower rate would 'raise Federal tax revenue by $50 billion' was asserted in its own findings without supporting analysis; permanent rate cuts of this size typically reduce revenue unless they trigger an unusual surge of repatriated profits.
A permanent low rate on foreign earnings would reward companies that shift profits and operations offshore, putting domestic-focused businesses that pay the full rate at a competitive disadvantage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a large, permanent tax cut to one concentrated group — multinationals with foreign profits — while relying on an unverified claim that it would pay for itself. Even granting the sponsor's job-creation argument, the permanent 5% rate would structurally reward moving profits offshore and shift the burden to other taxpayers, and the bill never received any committee review or analysis to test its claims.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, got no hearing or vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Stockman (R-TX) introduced the bill on December 11, 2014, with no cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax legislation.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the federal treasury kept the higher rates on corporate foreign profits, and the bill's potential corporate beneficiaries gained nothing. No one lost anything of value, since the bill never came close to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury; corporations gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no recorded opposition because it never reached a hearing or a vote; it also drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan bloc ever took a position on it.

industries.note: The bill would permanently cut their tax on foreign earnings from as high as 35% to a flat 5%, freeing roughly a trillion dollars in offshore profits. Because it died, they gained nothing, but a similar structure was later adopted in narrower forms.

These companies pay the full corporate rate on their U.S. earnings and generally have no foreign profits to shelter. The bill would have tilted the field further toward multinationals relative to them.
